To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) dose modifying agents may increase the probability of local control of human tumor by radiotherapy, but (ii) clinical benefit depends upon the steepness of the dose response curve for the tumor, (iii) a dose modifying agent with a modifying factor of at most 1.03 would be necessary to detect a clinical benefit, even in a large trial, and (iv) a dose modifying factor at least 1 to greater than 1 is required for clinical detection.

the dose response curve for local control by irradiation of human tumors is steep, and that a dose increment of at least 35% is necessary to achieve a 20% increase in local control.

The main takeaway from our work is that
dose-response curves for human tumors are steep, and that clinical trials must be designed with these curves in mind.
clinical trials of dose-modifying agents must be carefully designed to detect the clinical benefit of such agents.
dose modifying agents will be most effective in clinical trials when they are used to escalate the dose of the radiation therapy.
